title: Kinematics in one and two dimensions
note: Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. With constant acceleration, four equations link x, v, a, and t. In projectile motion the horizontal and vertical motions are independent: horizontal velocity stays constant while gravity accelerates the vertical motion at g = 9.80 m/s².

read.title: Two motions at once
text: Kinematics is the bookkeeping of motion: where an object is, how fast it moves, and how that changes. Velocity is the rate of change of position, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. On a graph, the slope of position versus time gives velocity, and the slope of velocity versus time gives acceleration. The area under a velocity–time graph gives displacement.
When acceleration is constant, a short set of equations predicts everything. The most useful are v = v₀ + at, x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at², and v² = v₀² + 2aΔx, which skips time entirely.

Projectile motion looks curved, but it is really two simple motions happening at once. Ignoring air resistance, nothing pushes the projectile sideways, so its horizontal velocity never changes. Vertically, gravity gives it a constant downward acceleration of 9.80 m/s², exactly as if it had been dropped. That is why a ball rolled off a table and a ball dropped from the same height hit the floor together: their vertical motions are identical. The horizontal speed only decides how far away the rolled ball lands. On level ground the range is greatest at a 45° launch, and complementary angles such as 30° and 60° land at the same spot.

q.q: Why do a rolled ball and a dropped ball land together?
o: The rolled ball has no acceleration
